title: Irish Stew
subtitle: Traditional lamb and potato stew
excerpt: The simplest, most satisfying stew in the Irish repertoire: neck of lamb, potato, onion, and carrots slow-cooked in a pale, herbed broth until the potato has thickened the stock and the lamb has yielded completely into tenderness.

recipe.sourceNotes: Irish stew is one of the oldest and most traditional dishes of Irish cuisine, originating as a peasant dish of the simplest available ingredients: mutton (old sheep), potatoes, and onions. The traditional version uses neck of mutton or lamb on the bone and has no carrots or other additions; the more widely made modern version adds carrot and turnip. The defining characteristic of authentic Irish stew is that it is pale and unclouded (lamb rather than brown beef broth, no browning of the meat, and potatoes that thicken the broth as they cook without adding flour). The stew improves considerably the day after it is made as the fat sets and can be lifted off and the flavours consolidate.

content.text: Traditional Irish stew does not brown the meat; this produces the characteristic pale broth. The potatoes should be a floury variety that will partially break down into the stock, thickening it naturally. Use neck of lamb on the bone if you can find it; the collagen from the bone enriches the broth considerably.

items.preparation: bone-in neck or shoulder; cut into pieces

content.text: Place the lamb pieces, onion, and carrot in a large, heavy pot. Add the stock, bay leaves, thyme, salt, and pepper. The stock should just cover the meat; add water if necessary.
Bring to a gentle simmer, skim any foam, and cover. Cook over the lowest heat for 1 hour.

Add the potatoes, cover again, and cook for a further 40 to 45 minutes until the potatoes are very tender and have partially dissolved into the broth, thickening it. Taste and adjust the seasoning. Scatter with parsley. Serve in deep bowls with crusty bread.
